entries.title: 12th heat-related death reported in Cook County tied to summer temperatures
entries.summary: <p>A 12th person has died from heat-related causes tied to this summer's extreme heat, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Jesus Rodriguez, 33, died July 17 due to hyperthermia and environmental heat exposure, in addition to cocaine toxicity, according to the medical examiner's office. He’s the youngest of the dozen deaths tied to the heat this year.</p><p>Cook County has had more deaths related to the heat in 2026 than any other year in the last decade, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis</u></a> of medical examiner data. Nine of the 12 have been Chicago residents, and almost all have been on the South Side. All but one of the deaths happened in July. The first heat-related death this year was recorded July 1.</p><p>The county has seen previous years with several heat-related deaths. Cook County recorded six deaths each in 2019 and 2022.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-840000" name="html-embed-module-840000"></a><div style="min-height:531px" id="datawrapper-vis-WIr6T"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WIr6T/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-WIr6T"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WIr6T/full.png" alt="Twelve people have died so far this year in Cook County from heat-related causes, the most in at least a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The next most recent heat death happened Tuesday, when Otto Kedzior died of cardiovascular disease <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/05/cook-county-10th-heat-related-death-2026" target="_blank" ><u>complications and heat stress</u></a> in the 1000 block of South Wood Street, authorities said. He was 64.</p><p>But most of the deaths occurred during July’s several bouts of extreme heat.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/12/heat-stroke-record-death-chicago-cook-county-medical-examiner-office-stress-elderly-senior" >Greater Grand Crossing woman’s death caused by heat stroke, medical examiner’s office rules</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" >Oak Lawn man’s death tied to mid-July heat wave</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Claramont Little, of the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/12/heat-stroke-record-death-chicago-cook-county-medical-examiner-office-stress-elderly-senior" target="_blank" ><u>died early in the morning of July 2</u></a> in the same block where she lived, authorities. entries.title: IHSA suspends Jordan Lynch, puts Mount Carmel football on probation after rule violation
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois High School Association has suspended Mount Carmel football coach Jordan Lynch for two practices and put the school's football program on probation for the rest of the season. </p><p>The sanctions were levied after the team practiced in full pads earlier than state rules allow. </p><p>On Aug. 8, a local reporter posted a photo on X of Mount Carmel's football practice. The photograph appeared to show the Caravan players in full pads. The post was eventually deleted. Antioch assistant football coach Thor Patrick Swanson later shared a screenshot of the post on his X account. </p><p>IHSA rules don't allow full protective equipment and full contact until the sixth day of practice. High school football practices began on Aug. 5.</p><p>Lynch, a 2009 graduate of Mount Carmel and a Heisman Trophy finalist at NIU in 2013, declined to comment on the matter. He will sit out practices on Aug. 17 and 18.</p><p>According to the IHSA, Mount Carmel self-reported the violation on August 12 and "provided a corrective action plan and self-imposed sanctions." The IHSA accepted the sanctions. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ef0000" entries.title: Illinois sues Trump admin over its demands for CDL database information
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and more than 20 officials from other states sued the Trump administration Thursday over its demand for access to state databases used by states to grant commercial drivers licenses known as CDLs.</p><p>The Trump administration has threatened to cut more than $10 million in federal funding to the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators for not handing over the last five years of data from the Commercial Driver’s License Information System.</p><p>The database was created in the late 1980s to help states determine driver eligibility for CDLs across state lines.</p><p>The lawsuits claim the Trump administration is violating both state and federal law by creating its own version of the database without guardrails for the handling of sensitive information, such as social security numbers. The lawsuits claim the administration “has no legitimate need to take over this database of state records, and it failed to consult the states before making this drastic change.”</p><p></p><p>The U.S. Department of Transportation didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The database includes drivers’ names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers and the name of states that provided the record, and is owned by the states that create them, according to the lawsuit. More than 17 million drivers’ information would be shared with the Trump administration if the court rules in favor of the feds.</p><p>Additionally, Illinois and California state law require written permission from each state for the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators to share information it has collected from the states, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, whose department is in charge of maintaining data privacy compliance for Illinois records shared to the database, said the federal government was demanding an “unprecedented amount of state-owned, sensitive personal information” without “adequate legal justification.”</p><p></p>

entries.title: 6 tornadoes Tuesday make record-breaking 206 total this year in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>The National Weather Service has confirmed six tornadoes hit the Chicago area in Tuesday's storms, raising the state total to a record-breaking 206 twisters this year. </p><p>The tornadoes touched down in Homewood, Oswego, Wilmington, Mokena to Tinley Park, Orland Park to Munster, Indiana, and Monee to St. John, Indiana.</p><p>The weather service Thursday evening confirmed an EF1 tornado in Homewood, with winds between 86 and 110 mph. The twister began near Halsted Street, between 183rd and 187th streets, damaging a strip mall and several apartment buildings. It ended east of Illinois Route 394 south of Thornton-Lansing Road.</p><p>The worst of the tornadoes hit Monee and St. John, with wind speeds peaking around 115 mph, according to the weather service. </p><p>That twister was an EF2 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, which rates the strength and related damage for tornadoes. Of the remaining five, four were classified as EF1 and one was EF0, officials said. An EF5 is the highest rating.</p><p>More than eight months into 2026, Illinois has already broken the record for most tornadoes recorded in a single year, shattering the previous record of 142 in 2024. </p><p>The total may climb with more severe weather forecast for central Illinois. A severe thunderstorm watch with conditions that may spawn a couple of tornadoes was in effect for Kankakee, Bloomington and Champaign among other areas, according to the weather service. </p>

entries.title: Trump is every bit the dictator he promised to be
entries.summary: <p>It was already one of the most clownish (if sinister) moments in the Trump administration — the Department of Justice actually brought criminal charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn for sabotaging the president's big, beautiful reflecting pool. It then dropped them for legal reasons that amounted to: "We screwed up."</p><p>But now we learn that Donald Trump can't let it go. The Wall Street Journal reports that the White House is pressuring the DOJ to revisit the case. Wonder if Todd Blanche will "talk the president out of it." (Just kidding.)</p><p>This is Trump's America. Hearn was cycling around the D.C. monuments and stopped to examine the very-much-in-the-news green swamp. The next thing he knew, he was being charged with felony vandalism. Just pause there for a second. This is police-state stuff. Don't let the fact that it was a false accusation about a fake offense regarding a trivial matter distract you. On one level, it seems cartoonish, but Hearn and three others were charged with real crimes (three misdemeanors and one felony). They had to get lawyers. One lost his job after his arrest and was forced to move out of his home. All of this because the Dim Leader was embarrassed when his pet project went wrong.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6a0000" name="module-6a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Hearn reached his hand into the water, according to Trump's post, and transformed Trump's expensively renovated "American flag blue" pool into a green, slimy mess with pieces of lining floating to the surface. That's some hand. Or did he sneak in under cover of darkness with a huge knife and make a 300-yard gash on the bottom of the pool? Trump didn't say. He was in tantrum mode and remains there.</p><p><i>Vandals! They are making me look ridiculous. They must pay</i>.</p><p>Every day that passes brings Trump closer to Captain Queeg of "The Caine Mutiny." Queeg ran over his own tow cable, had a nervous tick that involved ball bearings and was obsessed with his stash of strawberries, but he was at least able to command a ship, which is more than can be said of the president.</p><p>There are darker parallels, too. Failing leaders often seek scapegoats. Idi Amin blamed Asian immigrants for his nation's woes. The Ottomans blamed the Armenians for their poor showing in World War I. The focus on vandals, though, suggests no one more than Josef Stalin, who invented a whole category of crime, "wrecking," to deflect blame for his idiotic economic catastrophes. Trump is no Stalin — he's not as smart for one thing. But he would surely have no moral qualms about Stalin if the old monster were around today. Trump would probably describe him as a "tough guy" who gets results. No trouble about trials, just execute suspected criminals. Trump has praised China and the Philippines for precisely this, and in the Caribbean is carrying out that vicious policy on suspected drug smugglers (or anyone in a boat). Trump would have admired Stalin's "strength."</p><p>Just as Trump's own incompetence caused the reflecting pool renovation to fail, Stalin's own policies — forced collectivization of agriculture, hyper-rapid industrialization and rigid five-year plans — caused whole industries and sectors to fail. Scapegoats were required. Thus began the "wrecking" trials. Were mines having explosions? Arrest the engineers! Were there high rates of industrial accidents? Arrest the "saboteurs"! It began in the Donbas region of what is now Ukraine, where Stalin's henchmen arrested 53 mine engineers and managers and charged them with conspiring with the exiled and expropriated former owners to wreck the Soviet economy. Nikolai Krylenko, the prosecutor, accused them of "spoiling machinery, undermining the revolution's fuel supplies, inveigling the Soviet government into wasteful expenditures; preparations to destroy the coal industry as soon as war or intervention started." Seven got the death penalty. They were the first of hundreds of thousands (millions more would perish for other political crimes in the Gulag). Stalin used the trials to redirect public anger about hunger and shortages, but also to undermine and eventually eliminate his political rivals.</p><h3>Anti-science </h3><p>And while we're on the subject of Stalin, there's another aspect of late Trumpism that resembles the communist dystopia — the anti-science mania. Trump just issued an executive order on childhood vaccines that rivals Stalin's embrace of Lysenkoism. Trofim Lysenko was an agronomist who rejected Mendelian genetics in favor of his own theories — which happened to fit better into the Communist Party's concept of how the world works. He argued that acquired characteristics (like resistance to cold) could be inherited. If that were true, agricultural yields could be doubled or tripled or quadrupled in just a year or two. Lysenko framed his theories in communist jargon, denouncing Mendelian genetics as "bourgeois." American scientists who relied on fruit flies for research (due to their extremely short life spans) Lysenko denounced as "fly lovers and people haters."</p><p>Stalin, and later Mao, swallowed this lie whole and imposed it upon hundreds of millions of Russians and Chinese. Anyone can make a mistake, right? Except this politicization of science led to the worst famines in the 20th century, condemning tens of millions to slow starvation.</p><p>Trump's attacks on vaccines are very much in the same spirit, utterly divorced from reality and capable of causing great suffering (though not on the scale of Russian and Chinese famines).</p><p>We don't yet know how many more Americans will face the loss of their liberty due to the perversion of the Justice Department under Blanche. We do not know how many children will die of completely avoidable diseases due to the state-imposed quackery of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Trump. But we do know that as Trump prepares to denounce the Democrats as communists in the lead-up to November, few resemble them as much as he.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2d0000" name="module-2d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Texas gun ruling affirms limits of Congress' power
entries.summary: <p>Second Amendment groups <a class="Link" href="https://www.firearmspolicy.org/federal-court-strikes-major-blow-against-national-firearms-act-in-fpc-backed-lawsuit" target="_blank" >applauded</a> last week after a federal judge in Texas <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/06/a-federal-judge-rejects-national-firearms-act-regulations-saying-their-tax-rationale-no-longer-applies/" target="_blank" >ruled</a> that several national firearm regulations were unconstitutional. But the decision did not hinge on gun rights. Rather, it affirmed a <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/enumerated_powers" target="_blank" >broader principle</a>: The federal government's powers are limited to those explicitly granted by the Constitution.</p><p>The case involved the <a class="Link" href="https://www.atf.gov/media/25121/download" target="_blank" >National Firearms Act</a>, a 1934 law that targeted weapons and accessories thought to be favored by criminals. Because that law was framed as a revenue measure, U.S. District Judge James Hendrix <a class="Link" href="https://assets.nationbuilder.com/firearmspolicycoalition/pages/15027/attachments/original/1785949942/2026.08.05_136_OPINION.pdf" target="_blank" >held</a>, Congress fatally undermined the constitutional rationale for some of its provisions by eliminating the federal taxes on making and transferring sound suppressors, short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns.</p><p>Congress did that last year, when it approved a <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/1" target="_blank" >law</a> that retained the National Firearms Act's taxes on machine guns and "destructive devices" such as bombs and grenades but <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/07/gun-rights-groups-welcome-the-demise-of-illogical-and-constitutionally-dubious-federal-firearm-taxes/" target="_blank" >repealed</a> the taxes on all other products covered by the law. Given that change, Hendrix concluded, the reporting, registration and record-keeping requirements for the latter set of products, which ostensibly were aimed at facilitating revenue collection, could no longer be justified by the tax power that Congress invoked when it passed the law 92 years ago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2a0000" name="module-2a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>That rationale for the National Firearms Act, which was enacted as part of the Internal Revenue Code, may seem puzzling, since Congress has long relied on its power to regulate interstate commerce as an all-purpose license to legislate. But in 1934, legislators did not think that power was broad enough to authorize outright bans on politically disfavored products, an idea that would not gain currency until after the Supreme Court began <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2024/07/14/congress-can-regulate-virtually-anything/" target="_blank" >stretching</a> the commerce clause beyond recognition.</p><p>Instead of banning the listed weapons, Congress imposed a $200 tax on their production and transfer. That tax, which is equivalent to about $5,000 today, was meant to be prohibitive.</p><p>Attorney General Homer Cummings explained the need for that roundabout approach when he <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/NFA-1934-House.pdf#page=11" target="_blank" >testified</a> in favor of the National Firearms Act. Although Congress "of course" had "no inherent police powers to go into certain localities and deal with local crime," he said, it could still use "the power of taxation" to restrict weapons it viewed as especially dangerous.</p><p>"If we made a statute absolutely forbidding any human being to have a machine gun," Cummings explained, "you might say there is some constitutional question involved. But when you say, 'We will tax the machine gun,' and when you say that the absence of a license showing payment of the tax has been made indicates that a crime has been perpetrated, you are easily within the law."</p><p>Congress had taken a similar approach when it approved the <a class="Link" href="https://www.naabt.org/documents/harrison_narcotics_tax_act_1914.pdf" target="_blank" >Harrison Narcotics Tax Act</a> of 1914, which effectively prohibited nonmedical use of opiates and cocaine. It would likewise rely on "the power of taxation" to justify a <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-50/pdf/STATUTE-50-Pg551-2.pdf" target="_blank" >de facto national ban</a> on cannabis in 1937.</p><p>The Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep276/usrep276332/usrep276332.pdf" target="_blank" >blessed</a> that pretext in 1928, upholding the Harrison Act on the grounds that it raised "substantial revenue," consistent with its advertised purpose. But as Hendrix noted, Congress broke that thin reed when it eliminated the taxes on most National Firearms Act-regulated products.</p><p>The Trump administration argued that the act's regulations could still be justified under the commerce clause. Hendrix, a Trump appointee, <a class="Link" href="https://assets.nationbuilder.com/firearmspolicycoalition/pages/15027/attachments/original/1785949942/2026.08.05_136_OPINION.pdf" target="_blank" >disagreed</a>, saying the government "cannot employ post-hoc justifications to save a statute based on an enumerated power that Congress never invoked."</p><p>Nowadays, of course, Congress relies on the commerce clause to enact all sorts of regulations that were once viewed as beyond its scope, including laws criminalizing conduct that is neither interstate nor commercial. </p><p>"If Congress can regulate this under the commerce clause," Justice Clarence Thomas <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Gonzales-v.-Raich.pdf#page=57" target="_blank" >warned</a> in a 2005 case involving medical marijuana grown and consumed in California, "then it can regulate virtually anything — and the federal government is no longer one of limited and enumerated powers."</p><p>Hendrix's decision is a welcome reminder of that fundamental principle. But since 1934, Congress has found a new excuse to justify almost anything it wants to do.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-280000" name="module-280000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Remembering Haym Salomon, the Revolutionary War hero memorialized in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>On East Wacker Drive and North Wabash Avenue, not far from the heart of Chicago, three bronze figures stand together in a grouping most people pass without a second glance. At the center of the <a class="Link" href="https://webapps1.chicago.gov/landmarksweb/web/landmarkdetails.htm?lanId=1323" target="_blank" >Heald Square Monument</a> is George Washington. On his right stands Robert Morris, the superintendent of finance of the Continental Congress. On his left, there’s a Polish Jewish immigrant named Haym<b> </b>Salomon.</p><p>The statue has stood since 1941. Salomon's contribution is still older and larger than the monument suggests. As America celebrates its 250th birthday this year, Salomon's story is worthy of celebration.</p><p>Salomon was born around 1740 in Leszno, Poland, into a Jewish family that knew, by long inheritance, that the world could close in at any moment. He was brilliantly educated, fluent in eight or nine languages and possessed an extraordinary financial acumen. He immigrated to New York in 1772, just as the political storm that would become the Revolution was gathering.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1a0000" name="module-1a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>When the war came, Salomon did not wait on the sidelines. He became an agent for the patriot cause, was captured by the British, imprisoned and escaped — then captured again. He nearly died for the proposition that human beings could govern themselves.</p><p>But the part of his story that changes everything is financial. The Continental Congress was chronically, embarrassingly broke. Washington's soldiers were shoeless at Valley Forge, in part because the government that sent them there could not pay them. Robert Morris, scrambling to keep the Revolution solvent, turned repeatedly to one man: Haym Salomon.</p><p>What followed was one of the most consequential acts of quiet patriotism in American history. Salomon became the primary broker of the Continental cause — raising loans, negotiating bills of exchange and personally advancing money to the men who would shape the nation. He subsidized James Madison directly; Madison could not afford to remain in Philadelphia to serve in the Continental Congress without Salomon's support. He funded Thaddeus Kosciuszko, the Polish general who had crossed an ocean to fight for liberty. Salomon gave, and gave, and gave again.</p><p>How was such a man rewarded for his remarkable service to this country? </p><p>Not well. The loans were never repaid — not in his lifetime, not to his heirs. Salomon died in January 1785, only 13 years after coming to this land. He was 44 years old. He died in poverty, his estate worth almost nothing, and his family left with debts instead of assets. The Constitution he helped make possible was ratified two years after his death, the Bill of Rights, four years after that.</p><p>I am a rabbi, and in the weeks leading us to the semiquincentennial, our Torah reading fell on a portion called B'haalotcha — a Hebrew word that means, roughly, "when you cause the lights to go up." It describes the kindling of the great menorah in the Mishkan<i>, </i>the ancient portable sanctuary. But the Torah's phrasing is deliberate: not "light the menorah," but <i>cause </i>the flames to rise. The medieval commentator Rashi notes that the phrasing served as instruction to Aaron, the high priest,to hold the flame to each wick until the light rose on its own — and only then to step back.</p><p>There is something in that image I cannot shake when I think about Salomon. He did not live to see the light rise. He held the flame to the wick at enormous personal cost — his fortune, his freedom and ultimately his life — and trusted that if he held it long enough, the flame would find its own life. It did, and we are standing in that light today.</p><p>America’s 250th anniversary has arrived in a moment of fierce political division. Arguments about who this country is for, who it has always been for, and who gets to claim its founding promise have never been louder. Into that argument, Salomon's story inserts a quiet and clarifying fact: The American Revolution was not sustained by famous names alone. It was sustained by many hands, among them the hand of a Polish Jewish immigrant who asked for nothing in return.</p><p>The next time you are walking at Wacker Drive and Wabash Avenue, stop at that statue. Look at the Jewish man standing at the shoulder of the father of our country and take a moment to consider the many overlooked people whose contributions helped to create and sustain the country that we call home.</p><p><i>Rabbi Michael Siegel is senior rabbi at Anshe Emet Synagogue in Chicago.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d70000" name="module-d70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Weapons of mass distraction
entries.summary: <p>Once again the Chicago Air and Water Show is about to be inflicted upon the city. The event, which features civilian demonstrations but is mostly centered on the military, is reminiscent of the "bread and circuses" of another failed empire. Just as with the Romans, we peasants are treated to a spectacle to distract us from the reality of the abject impoverishment of the social safety net and the abandonment of the poor.</p><p>The weapons dealers responsible for the cacophony on the lakefront of thundering jets have been gifted with billions of tax dollars for the research and development of these weapons of mass destruction.</p><p>The billions spent on the military could have gone a long way to educating our children and feeding the poor.</p><p>It would be wise for the throngs gathering on the lakefront to reflect on what they are sacrificing for their day at the beach.</p><p><i>Edward David Juillard, Morgan Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-970000" name="module-970000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Highlight accessible services at Air and Water Show</h3><p>The city of Chicago does a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dca/supp_info/air_water_show_visit.html" target="_blank" >great service to its citizens</a> by providing audio description, as well as American Sign Language, for Chicago Air and Water Show attendees who are blind, have low vision or are hearing-impaired. It's unfortunate the Sun-Times didn't mention this in its article about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/08/11/what-to-know-about-the-2026-chicago-air-and-water-show" >what to know about the show.</a></p><p>As the population ages, blindness, low vision and hearing issues increases with deleterious effect. There's stigma around losing sensory abilities There's very little education around what accessibility services are, why and how to get them. The Sun-Times can help.</p><p>Consider what a positive impact giving accessibility information would have on your readers.</p><p><i>Colette Martin-Wilde, West Ridge</i></p><h3>Reflecting on Trump</h3><p>President Donald Trump’s continuing tantrum over the recent fetid mess in the <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6019582-contractor-error-reflecting-pool-renovations/" target="_blank" >Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool</a> brings to mind an ironically relatable literary reflection in Oscar Wilde’s novel "The Picture of Dorian Gray."</p><p>The big difference is that Dorian Gray could keep the curdling portrait of his own personal vices hidden away in his attic. But the symbolic reflection of Trump’s shoddy statesmanship and moral defects, represented by the pool’s<i> </i>algae infestation, was nationally on view for all to see.</p><p>No wonder the president is beside himself.</p><p><i>Steven Doloff, Gold Coast</i></p><h3>Siren sounds</h3><p>Street-level sirens in the River North and Streeterville areas frequently reach 110 decibels. According to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.audiology.org/consumers-and-patients/hearing-and-balance/noise-induced-hearing-loss/" target="_blank" >American Academy of Audiology</a>, hearing loss can occur above 85 decibels for anyone on adjoining sidewalks, especially babies and children. Surely this is increased by reflection off tall buildings. This is a public health hazard that the city needs to address.</p><p><i>Chris C. Kovich, River North</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Support for Some Charities Can Result in a Busy Mailbox
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Do charities and nonprofits share or sell donor information? For years, maybe decades, I've made quarterly contributions to two well-known charities for children's cancer research hospitals, and I truly believe in what they do. However, over the last few years, I have started receiving an increasing number of requests for money.</p><p>One continues to send me quarterly requests, and I promptly write a check. But the other one started sending mailings every month, then every week and now multiple times a week, not to mention the newer "legacy program" (naming them in my will). I have also received messages on my landline phone, text messages and emails, and none of this contact information has previously been given to them, only my mailing address.</p><p>Today, I received seven pieces of mail. Six were requests for donations, five of which I'm not familiar with, and I have gotten the feeling my name and address have been sold or shared with other nonprofits. It feels to me as if they're spending the money I've donated to print and mail even more requests, and I'll no longer donate to them. I will increase the amount of donations to local school programs.</p><p>Is there a way to get them to stop mailing me? Maybe they'll read this and think twice about bombarding people to the point they no longer will support them. — <i>FULL MAILBOX IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR FULL MAILBOX:</b> According to Give.org, businesses and charitable organizations do sell their clients' or donors' contact information to other organizations. If your name is on a list of subscribers to a special interest magazine or buyers of a certain product or service, it may wind up on a list used by various charities.</p><p>You may be able to lessen the onslaught of appeals you receive by writing directly to the charities whose mail you don't want and asking them to delete your name from the mailing lists they rent or exchange. (A Better Business Bureau standard requires that a charity offer contributors an opt-out opportunity in its appeals at least once a year.)</p><p>Enclose the mailing label or return card that came with your appeal when you contact the charity. Be sure to add the correct postage to their envelope on which you have written "delete my name" or "return to sender" because charities' nonprofit mailing rates do not pay for returns.</p><p>For more information on this subject, visit Give.org.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mom passed last year. I'm 50, and my brother is 52. He has never been good with money. He's gullible and lets people take advantage of him. He will not let me help him.</p><p>Should I get a guardianship for him or let him fend for himself? We already have a rocky relationship. I worry that taking control of his finances will make it worse. However, I would feel guilty if he mismanaged his money, and I think Mom would want me to help him. What should I do? — <i>MY BROTHER'S KEEPER</i></p><p><b>DEAR BROTHER'S KEEPER:</b> Please accept my sympathy for the loss of your mother. It's unfortunate these questions weren't settled before her passing. Because your brother needs someone to look out for him, and you are the only one who can fill this role with his best interests in mind, discuss this with an attorney. Of course, it will need to be explained to your brother. Don't put off talking with him, even if the subject is uncomfortable for one or both of you.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago’s ‘Soul City’ is still waiting for its landmark
entries.summary: <p>Since 2020, residents of Chicago’s Austin neighborhood have been waiting for the city to erect a gateway arch at the entrance of its Soul City Corridor, the stretch of Chicago Avenue from Austin Boulevard to Cicero Avenue.</p><p>They were thrilled when an artist, Bernard Williams, was selected and renderings were drawn up. And last year, Illinois designated a larger segment of Austin as Soul City, <a class="Link" href="https://dceo.illinois.gov/oe3/il-state-designated-cultural-districts.html" target="_blank" ><u>one of 15 official cultural districts</u></a> in the state, paving the way for $200,000 in additional monies to boost the neighborhood.</p><p>But the gateway construction has stalled, leaving the burgeoning development of Black business, arts and culture unidentifiable to those driving from the west suburbs into the city. The delay over a single symbol illustrates how bureaucratic the process to create a cultural district in Illinois can be.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-220000" name="image-220000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c2a6e9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F77%2Ff76ea3fa4487a6511c637cdea0fd%2Fquarterzip-120825-014.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9b9e1a5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F77%2Ff76ea3fa4487a6511c637cdea0fd%2Fquarterzip-120825-014.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c4fe4d2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F77%2Ff76ea3fa4487a6511c637cdea0fd%2Fquarterzip-120825-014.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Event co-organizer Corey DooleyJohnson smiles during the “Chicago Quarter Zip Link Up” at Shawn Michelle's Homemade Ice Cream in Bronzeville on the South Side, Sunday, Dec. 7, 2025. So to be able to have a gateway there says that we [now] care about the community.”<b> </b></p><p>In July, Mayor Brandon Johnson and the city's Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events told the Sun-Times that the project was still in the works, but he didn’t provide a timeline.</p><p>“This is something that's going to live in perpetuity,” said the mayor, an Austin resident who touted the corridor as a hallmark of his legacy. “That’s the hope, that every generation will see this as a symbol of the soul of Chicago. So we just want to make sure that depiction is something that accurately tells our story, but also speaks to our future.”</p><p>Soul City is technically bordered by North Avenue to the north, Madison Avenue to the south, Austin Avenue to the west and Cicero Avenue to the East. Though the City of Chicago has been slow to install the gateway, it has recently made investments into Austin, the third-most populous community area in Chicago, with the most Black residents. </p><p>Millions have been spent renovating Chicago Avenue and supporting the development of Black-owned businesses, mixed-income housing, health and workforce centers and arts organizations.<b> </b></p><p>While appreciative of those efforts, residents are eager to see “Soul City” prominently displayed. They view the moniker as a symbol of pride that will help shift negative narratives about the area. entries.title: Chicago police traffic stops plunge, again, but Black and Latino drivers still get pulled over far more
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Police Department made fewer traffic stops in 2025 than in the previous year and less than half the stops it made in 2023, according to a new report by the Illinois Department of Transportation, but Chicago police officers continued to pull over Black and Latino drivers at much higher rates than white drivers.</p><p>The Chicago Police Department reported 224,851 traffic stops in 2025, about 23.3% fewer than in 2024 and 58.0% less than in 2023.</p><p>IDOT uses two methods, or benchmarks, to measure the rates at which drivers are stopped. Those attempt to estimate the driving population or the total mileage driven within the jurisdiction of each law enforcement agency. By one measure, Black drivers were 3.6 times more likely than white drivers and Latino drivers were 2.85 times more likely than white drivers to be stopped by the Chicago police last year. By another measure, Black drivers were 5.6 times more likely and Latino drivers 6.9 times more likely to get stopped.</p><p>Most traffic stops made by the Chicago police last year, about 67.6%, were for non-moving violations, according to IDOT.</p><p>Those stops in particular have drawn flak, with some critics contending that police officers routinely use minor traffic violations as a pretext to stop drivers — and sometimes to search their vehicles — in hopes of uncovering more serious crimes.</p><p>A lot of traffic stops in Chicago are for things like expired plates, tinted windows and broken taillights, said Maya Simkin, an Appleseed Network Collaboration for Justice Fellow with Chicago Appleseed and a member of the Free2Move Coalition. “It's not about posing a genuine safety risk.”</p><p>Craig Futterman, a University of Chicago Law School professor who's a member of the state’s Racial Profiling Prevention and Data Oversight Board, said the police often view traffic stops as a way to fight crime.</p><p>“I don’t think that it is necessarily the case that departments are being evil," Futterman said. "It’s that they actually think this is a good crime-fighting tool and don’t want anyone to take that tool away from them."</p><p>He said "there’s also nefarious aspects of … this tool. It has created dramatic harm in communities as well as losses in public safety and losses of trust and confidence, or the absence of trust and confidence in police, if people feel that they are being harassed and targeted not because of what they’ve done but because of their race or ethnicity.”</p><p>Chicago police officials didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-bc0000" name="html-embed-module-bc0000"></a><div style="min-height:877px" id="datawrapper-vis-7PgsI"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7PgsI/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-7PgsI"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7PgsI/full.png" alt="Chicago police officers routinely pulled over Black and Latino drivers the most in 2025 (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In 2023, the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois sued the department over mass traffic stops of Black and Latino drivers. The lawsuit recently was certified as a class action, meaning the organization now represents all Black and Latino drivers who have been or will be pulled over by the Chicago police.</p><p>According to Alexandra Block, director of the ACLU's Criminal Legal Systems and Policing Project, the Chicago police have known about IDOT’s traffic stop reports but taken no significant action to address the issues raised. The ACLU has taken depositions of about 35 Chicago police officials, including seven former superintendents. Block said former Superintendents David Brown and Eddie Johnson testified they were aware of the reports.</p><p>“They receive copies every year, but they didn't make any changes in response to IDOT’s analysis,” Block said.</p><p>In his first months on the job, former Supt. Larry Snelling said he would reduce the department’s use of traffic stops. “There’s already been a reduction in traffic stops since I’ve taken over because the focus is different. My focus is [on] violent crimes and traffic safety,” Snelling said at a meeting of the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability in December 2023.</p><p>The reductions in CPD traffic stops during 2024 and 2025 occurred under Snelling’s watch, but the racial disparities remained. A federal judge has ordered Snelling to testify in court as part of the ACLU’s lawsuit against CPD.</p><p>Block and others have said the police department hasn’t reported all of its traffic stops to the state over the past few years, pre-dating the Snelling era. Block said data from the city of Chicago Office of Emergency Management and Communications showing the number of times that officers radioed into dispatch for a traffic stop indicates that the department made far more stops last year than it reported.</p><p>“What we know is that the number of stops reported has declined but that the Chicago Police Department failed to report more stops in 2025 than they did report,” Block said. “There were over 250,000 stops that they did not report.”</p><h3><b>Traffic stops up elsewhere in Illinois</b></h3><p>The Chicago police and law enforcement agencies statewide are required to report data about their traffic stops each year under a 2003 state law, originally proposed by then-state Sen. Barack Obama to assess potential racial bias in traffic stops. IDOT collects data from law enforcement agencies and contracts with outside groups to analyze the data.</p><p>Last year, among 963 law enforcement agencies in the state that made traffic stops, nearly one in every five did not report any data, according to the IDOT report. The percentage of agencies making stops but not reporting their data has increased the past two years, from 16.5% in 2023 to 18.4% in 2024 and to 19.5% in 2025.</p><p>In total, law enforcement agencies across Illinois conducted more than 2 million traffic stops last year, slightly more than the previous year. While traffic stops reported by CPD have decreased the past two years, stops made by all other police agencies in the state, collectively, have increased in each of the past five years. In 2025, excluding Chicago, law enforcement agencies in Illinois reported nearly 1.84 million traffic stops, a 48.9% increase from about 1.23 million reported in 2020, according to IDOT.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-520000" name="html-embed-module-520000"></a><div style="min-height:521px" id="datawrapper-vis-WmdVP"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WmdVP/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-WmdVP"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WmdVP/full.png" alt="Chicago police officers reported less traffic stops, even as police departments saw a statewide increase (Small multiple column chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Like Chicago, most police agencies in Illinois pulled over Black and Latino drivers at higher rates last year. Nearly 95% of all agencies that reported at least 50 stops had higher stop rates for Black drivers compared to white drivers. About 80% of all agencies had higher stop rates for Latino drivers compared to white drivers, according to IDOT.</p><p>But law enforcement agencies have routinely criticized the state’s methodology for determining traffic stop rates. More than 30 police agencies offered such comments in the IDOT report.</p><p>IDOT notes that researchers use a combination of data sources — including surveys from the U.S. Census Bureau, Illinois crash reports, driver’s license counts, employment data, traffic counts and other sources — to estimate the driving population and total mileage driven by motorists.</p><p>IDOT acknowledges the limitations of its benchmarks. “However elaborate these datasets may be, they can only approximate local traffic dynamics and necessarily rely on particular assumptions, which may not always be accurate,” the report says.</p><p>Futterman and other civil rights advocates are calling for an end to pretextual stops as a way to remedy the long-standing racial disparities.</p><p>“There’s a real addiction and a wrongful belief, in my view, that using pretext stops is an effective crime-fighting tool,” Futterman said. “It actually hurts the ability of police to effectively fight crime and gain the cooperation of community members to solve violent crime.”</p><p>Futterman points to research that followed traffic stops of the San Francisco Police Department from 2022 to 2025. San Francisco police banned pretextual traffic stops in 2024.</p><p>“Put plainly, the pretext ban policies did not result in fewer guns and drugs discovered, nor did they result in the apprehension of fewer criminals,” the Berkeley Public Policy Journal wrote in a February report about the research. “They did, however, result in fewer searches of Black and Hispanic drivers.”</p><p>Futterman said a similar reform could work in Illinois.</p><p>“Illinois, as a state, could prohibit police from pulling over people for low-level traffic violations when drivers don’t pose any immediate risk to public safety,” Futterman said.</p>

entries.title: Bears rookie Hayden Large's journey lives up to his name
entries.summary: <p>Bedridden for more than a month, Hayden Large found a favorite television show: “Friday Night Lights.”</p><p>Of course he did. It was where he wanted to be.</p><p>“Greatest show ever,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tight end said.</p><p>In 2019, Large tore his hamstring — and an egg-shaped piece of his pelvic bone along with it — in a scrimmage weeks before the start of his senior season at Unity Christian High School in Hudsonville, Mich. He spent 35 days on bed rest, though he’d sneak out to attend high school games, and wondered what would become of his football career.</p><p>He’d run for 1,300 yards and 12 touchdowns as a junior, winning the state championship. Now he feared he’d never play again.</p><p>“I was told,” he said, “I might not be the same.”</p><p>Seven years and six college seasons later, the 24-year-old will play his first NFL game Saturday when the Bears host the Browns.</p><p>“The story's a really redemptive story,” said Joel Penner, the head coach at NAIA Dordt University. “And it's fun to see.”</p><p>Lions receiver Isaac TeSlaa saw it up close. The two have been friends since third grade, when TeSlaa played guard and Large played running back. They went to the same high school, playing on a varsity squad of only 22 kids. They joined the basketball team together just to stay in shape.</p><p>TeSlaa was on the field when Large was tackled during the scrimmage. Large insisted on being propped up on a training bench to watch the end of it, wearing sunglasses to fight the glare, all without part of his pelvic bone.</p><p>When Large was bedridden, TeSlaa would stop by balloons to cheer him up. He knew his friend was struggling.</p><p>“That’s the time in our lives when everyone’s hanging out,” he said. “He had to be at home and hobbled around.”</p><p>They’d once dreamed of going to college together. TeSlaa agreed to play for Div. II Hillsdale. Large went to Dordt — the 2,000-person school was the only one to offer him a football spot. Even though it shared the same religious affiliation with his high school, Dordt, in the northwest corner of Iowa, felt far away from home. His dad, Forrest, nonetheless made the 12-hour drive for each game, watching his son turn into a small-college star.</p><p>By his sophomore year, Large’s coaches built plays specifically for him, moving him into the backfield or splitting him wide at receiver.</p><p>“He had that motor and that drive within,” Penner said.</p><p>In three seasons, he caught 62 passes for 950 yards and 12 touchdowns.</p><p>“I was just happy to play football at that moment,” Large said. “Anything I could get out of football, I wanted to.”</p><p>Large decided he wanted more. TeSlaa decided to transfer after three standout Div. II seasons, eventually landing at Arkansas. He talked to Large about making a similar leap.</p><p>“I felt I had to challenge myself at the Div. I level,” TeSlaa said. “I felt like he did too.”</p><p>Large decided to go. Iowa offered him a preferred walk-on spot. His name — the inspiration had nothing to do with Hayden Fry, Iowa’s legendary coach — and position made Large a cult hero in short order. He started twice at fullback in each of his first two years — “It’s a mindset thing,” he said — before emerging as a blocking-first tight end in 2025, his sixth college season. </p><p>It wasn’t until his final season that Abdul Hodge, the Hawkeyes’ tight ends coach, told him he might have a future in the NFL.</p><p>“He said, ‘You can make a niche for yourself if you get to the right team,’” he said.</p><p>Large knew that could be the Bears — and vice versa. Before the NFL draft began, coach Ben Johnson called Large and laid out the vision he had for him. When the Bears took tight end Sam Roush in Round 3, though, he feared Large would be discouraged from signing.</p><p>“He didn't bat an eye,” Johnson said. “This is where he wanted to be. To me, that speaks volumes about how he's wired. That has something to do with how he came — walk on at Iowa, earning playing time and going through the long, hard road. I really appreciate that.”</p><p>The Bears like taking Iowa blockers, including second-round rookie center Logan Jones in April. The Hawkeyes’ ground-it-out-style offense prepares them for Johnson’s scheme. Tight ends coach Jim Dray can appreciate the work ethic that got Large this far — “There’s a desire to do right,” he said — but few make it this far without it.</p><p>The 6-4, 250-pound Large is near the bottom of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/02/bears-training-camp-predict-53-man-roster-cut-day-ben-johnson-ryan-poles-caleb-williams-padded-practice-nfl" target="_blank" >seven-person tight end room</a> — but he knows what the Bears will be looking for against the Browns.</p><p>“Physicality,” he said.</p><p>TeSlaa tries to figure the odds of two high school teammates from a 22-man team playing major-college football, much less appearing in the NFL. It’s astronomical — but so were the odds of Large making it this far.</p><p>“I feel like this is going to be a great showcase for him,” TeSlaa said. “We’ve had talks about the immense pressure, but he’s in such a great spot mentally that he’s going to give his absolute all.”</p>

entries.title: Illinois' special prosecutors have strong political ties and little oversight
entries.summary: <p>On a cool September night in 2014, 18-year-old Pietro Mautino sped down a rural county road about 100 miles southwest of Chicago, his friend at the wheel of his bronze Kia sedan. The headlights were off.</p><p>Around 1:35 a.m., police pulled them over. The car reeked of cannabis, police reported.</p><p>An officer watched Mautino toss a plastic pill bottle into the back seat. Searching the car and Mautino’s black Prada bag, he inventoried a hydrocodone pill, 14 clonazepam pills, a baggie of marijuana, some hash oil and drug paraphernalia, according to police reports.</p><p>The son of longtime state Rep. Frank Mautino and a paid campaign staffer, Pietro Mautino was charged with two counts of unlawful possession of a controlled substance, a Class 4 felony with a recommended sentencing range of one to three years in prison for each count.</p><p>Because of the elder Mautino’s connections to prosecutors, the case was turned over to Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit, a team of state government attorneys who take charge in county courts across Illinois when local authorities are disqualified because of a potential conflict.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Frank Mautino speaks with reporters on the House floor in Springfield in January 2011.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Pietro Mautino’s case highlights the political ties of the Special Prosecution Unit’s leaders, who at times have their own conflicts of interest and political entanglements.</p><p>Before Pietro Mautino’s arrest, the Illinois State’s Attorney’s Association PAC, a political action committee that shared an address and leadership with the Special Prosecution Unit, made contributions to Frank Mautino’s campaign. Soon after, Mautino became the state auditor general, one of the few state officials with even nominal oversight over the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>The state agency housing the Special Prosecution Unit has long handed out no-bid contracts to political insiders and hired well-connected prosecutors, government records show. And the unit has shielded defendants with clout while its political allies helped protect the agency from public scrutiny by writing it out of the state’s public records law.</p><p>The charges against Pietro Mautino stalled for three years before a special prosecutor offered a plea deal that enabled him to avoid prison. Under the deal, he was sentenced to 24 months of special probation before the public case file was expunged, according to court records and news reports.</p><p>The special prosecutor handling the case, Dave Neal, explained the trial delays by saying police drug-testing labs had a backlog of more serious cases. A police report from downstate Peru shows lab testing was not conducted until 2017, more than two years into the prosecution. But the officer who handled the test says he would have done so sooner if asked by the prosecutor. Neal did not respond to requests for comment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9a0000" name="image-9a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/36ae72a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d3f91f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/45fb191/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lake County Special Prosecutor Dave Neal talks to a witness during the sentencing hearing for Daniel Baker at the Lake County courthouse in Waukegan Monday for the murder of 50-year-old Marina Aksman in her Vernon Hills home on April1, 2010. Frank Mautino had donated more than $5,500 to Towne’s campaigns in the years before his son’s prosecution, campaign finance data show, and news reports show Towne honored Mautino with an Outstanding Legislator Award in 2015.</p><h3><b>An agency hidden from public view</b></h3><p>The unit’s parent agency, the Illinois State’s Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor, or ILSAAP, was created in 1977 to help local prosecutors fight a flood of appeals from indigent prisoners. At the time, Illinois courts were expanding the rights of people who contested their convictions and lawmakers had created the Office of the State Appellate Defender to represent them. County state’s attorneys and their legislative allies created ILSAAP as a counterforce.</p><p>ILSAAP’s mission statement, then and now, is spelled out in its annual reports: “Keep convicted criminals behind bars.”</p><p>ILSAAP’s power has been expanded steadily over the past four decades as state lawmakers added a slew of new legal assignments to its now-$36 million annual budget: assisting state’s attorneys with property tax cases, helping distribute drug forfeiture funds, training county prosecutors on the Pretrial Fairness Act and other laws — and deploying special prosecutors when local officials have a conflict of interest.</p><p>But ILSAAP’s oversight structure creates an apparent conflict of interest that shadows the Special Prosecution Unit’s work.</p><p>The “independent” special prosecutors are governed by a board of 10 elected state’s attorneys who rely on ILSAAP to defend them on appeals and replace them with special prosecutors when they or their offices have a conflict.</p><p>The board establishes the agency’s rules, regulations and procedures, and governs all aspects of ILSAAP’s operation, agency publications say. But the public minutes from recent meetings show only the barest oversight; the March 2026 meeting lasted just seven minutes.</p><p>That’s about the only scrutiny the agency gets.</p><p>In 2010, as ILSAAP was facing public records requests about the Special Prosecution Unit, ILSAAP leaders pulled off a legislative sleight of hand to shield themselves from public view.</p><p>ILSAAP was initially formed as a commission within Illinois’ executive branch, making it subject to the Freedom of Information Act, which requires government agencies to provide documents and information to the public upon request.</p><p>But then-state Sen. William Haine, a former Madison County state’s attorney who served as ILSAAP’s point person in the General Assembly, quietly introduced a bill making ILSAAP part of the judicial branch, which is exempt from FOIA in Illinois.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c90000" name="image-c90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4468a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2976x1670+0+345/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2Fb1%2F1195b4d94e3eb0398f6dc78e083d%2Fmedical-marijuana-llinois.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9dab4d1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2976x1670+0+345/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2Fb1%2F1195b4d94e3eb0398f6dc78e083d%2Fmedical-marijuana-llinois.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/21807ae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2976x1670+0+345/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2Fb1%2F1195b4d94e3eb0398f6dc78e083d%2Fmedical-marijuana-llinois.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois Sen. He never even used words like “judicial” or “FOIA,”, legislative transcripts show.</p><p>Instead, Haine told fellow lawmakers he was making an “update” that “allows for a different configuration in the board and a few other things that updates the office.”</p><p>When ILSAAP’s exemption from FOIA was later debated in court in 2013, the Illinois’ Appellate Court ridiculed ILSAAP’s new designation as an arm of the state courts. Calling ILSAAP a judicial agency was like saying a dog had five legs because you counted its tail as one leg, the court wrote in Uphoff v. Grosskopf, citing a quip from Abraham Lincoln.</p><p>ILSAAP “is, in fact, in no sense a judicial agency of state government,” the court wrote. ILSAAP’s exemption from public records laws.</p><p>The maneuver deprives Illinois citizens of their basic right to be informed about the workings of a critical government agency, says Steve Helle, a Today, ILSAAP is still part of the judiciary on paper, but the state Supreme Court provides no oversight or even interaction with ILSAAP or the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>“There’s nothing in the Illinois State’s Attorneys Appellate Prosecutors Act that requires the [Administrative Office of the Illinois Courts] or Supreme Court to provide oversight,” says Illinois courts spokesperson Christopher Bonjean.</p><p>ILSAAP Director Patrick Delfino and Board Chair Ben Goetten did not respond to requests for comment.</p><h3><b>Political contributions and no-bid contracts</b></h3><p>ILSAAP has had just two directors in the past 35 years.</p><p>Former Greene County State’s Attorney Norbert Goetten took over the agency in 1991. He was succeeded in 2008 by his top aide, Patrick Delfino, a former director of planning and special projects for the Cook County state’s attorney’s office who helped write the legislation that created ILSAAP.</p><p>Both were accused of misconduct in the 1990s, when then-state Auditor General William Holland scrutinized ILSAAP’s use of contracts and state phones. Holland reported in a public audit that ILSAAP no-bid contractors were being paid with little evidence they did any actual work, and ILSAAP staffers were using their state phones to make personal long-distance calls.</p><p>Delfino agreed to give up an accumulated 55 vacation days to pay for private calls allegedly made on a state phone, including calls to a girlfriend, the State Journal-Register reported in 1995. Goetten said at the time that the 55 days amounted to “way more” than the cost of Delfino’s personal phone calls.</p><p>ILSAAP contract records were subpoenaed by the U.S. attorney’s office, with the FBI interviewing Goetten, the State Journal-Register reported, but no charges were filed.</p><p>Goetten survived the scrutiny by the auditor general and the FBI, and he and his family deepened their ties to ILSAAP.</p><p>His son, Jersey County State’s Attorney Ben Goetten, has served as chairman of ILSAAP’s Board of Governors since 2020. Another son, Matthew Goetten, is an ILSAAP special prosecutor, while Goetten’s grandson, Connor Goetten, is an ILSAAP staff attorney.</p><p>Norbert Goetten ran a private Jersey County law practice while running ILSAAP. He was chair of ILSAAP’s political action committee and contributed more than $10,000 of his own money to Illinois politicians.</p><p>His son Ben was later treasurer of the PAC, which began making political donations to legislative allies while Goetten was in charge of ILSAAP. From 2006 to 2015, the PAC donated $6,200 to Haine, who sponsored the legislation exempting ILSAAP from FOIA.</p><p>ILSAAP continues to award no-bid consulting and legal services contracts to political insiders and lawyers with spotty records. ILSAAP and the contractors declined to comment.</p><p>In the most recent fiscal year, the agency awarded no-bid contracts to Lisa Duarte, a former top aide to Gov. entries.title: Clout, conflicts of interest cloud the work of Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit
entries.summary: <p>The former assistant state’s attorney charged with murder.</p><p>The judge caught driving drunk.</p><p>The clerk accused of skimming government funds.</p><p>When local prosecutors might have political or personal ties to a defendant, the state brings in an elite squad of government attorneys: the Illinois Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>They are supposed to be lawyers beyond reproach.</p><p>Instead, the unit has been clouded by allegations of corruption, misconduct and conflicts of interest.</p><p>The two dozen lawyers of Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit are mostly former county state’s attorneys, many with powerful political connections. All are white, most are men.</p><p>Since its creation in the 1980s, the unit has been the primary way criminal cases in Illinois are handled when local state’s attorneys are disqualified because of conflicts. Its prosecutors took on more than 1,000 cases in 2024, far more than were pursued through other methods of appointing special prosecutors, including referrals to the state attorney general, private attorneys or prosecutors from neighboring counties.</p><p>But the Special Prosecution Unit has been responsible for miscarriages of justice including withholding evidence and favorable treatment of political insiders, as well as conflicts of interest and ethical breaches.</p><p>To examine the Special Prosecution Unit, Injustice Watch reviewed thousands of pages of court documents and interviewed dozens of people, including defendants who were wrongly charged, victims who never saw justice, unit veterans and legal experts.</p><p>Here are the key findings:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-c2a08352-9716-11f1-978c-7f7413ccaf70"><li>Special prosecutors withheld exculpatory evidence that could have set murder defendant Curtis Lovelace free. The former Adams County prosecutor was acquitted in 2017 for the murder of his wife after spending 21 months in jail, but the misguided prosecution <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/shadow-prosecutors/2026/prosecutorial-misconduct-curtis-lovelace/" target="_blank" >tore through his community and life</a>. </li><li>In 2014, special prosecutors were called in after police arrested the son of Frank Mautino, who had represented LaSalle County for nearly a quarter-century as a state lawmaker. A political action committee tied to the Special Prosecution Unit made donations to Mautino’s campaign fund and <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/shadow-prosecutors/2026/political-ties-little-oversight/" target="_blank" >supported his appointment as state auditor general</a>, one the of the few state offices with a limited watchdog function over the unit. </li><li>After 31-year-old mother of three Megan Wells was killed in a 2016 Rock River boat crash by an allegedly drunk boater, special prosecutors dropped most of the charges as part of a plea deal, <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/shadow-prosecutors/2026/conflicts-of-interest-powerful-defendants/" target="_blank" >allowing the defendant, a well-connected pharmacist, to walk free</a>. The lead prosecutor never publicly disclosed a professional connection to the local state’s attorney he replaced.</li></ul><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-720000" name="image-720000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ac9be93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5520x3098+0+291/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F83%2Fc9%2F99ad70b54bc1b283629e0a85583d%2Feonri-cst-071714-2.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0a553f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5520x3098+0+291/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F83%2Fc9%2F99ad70b54bc1b283629e0a85583d%2Feonri-cst-071714-2.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/056c713/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5520x3098+0+291/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F83%2Fc9%2F99ad70b54bc1b283629e0a85583d%2Feonri-cst-071714-2.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Rep. Frank Mautino, right, speaks during a Legislative Audit Commission hearing in July 2014.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In other cases, the Special Prosecution Unit seemed to go after low-level political scapegoats, failing to secure convictions, but leaving devastation in its wake.</p><p>In 2007, special prosecutors filed four felony charges against McLean County Clerk Peggy Ann Milton for allegedly misusing a roll of postage stamps to support a charity and asking a county employee to drive her son home on county time. The jury quickly acquitted Milton, but her life was upended.</p><p>“My son was young at the time, and [the prosecutor] intimidated him,” Milton says. "Once something like that is so public, especially in a small community, it's difficult for you to get past it.”</p><p>The special prosecutors responsible for these and other questionable cases all remain on the job today. Others were hired by the Special Prosecution Unit despite alleged impropriety in their past roles.</p><p>William Elward joined the Special Prosecution Unit after a 2016 state inspector general's report found he submitted false time sheets while working for the Illinois attorney general’s office, improperly billing the state for hundreds of hours when he was in fact moonlighting as a law teacher out of state.</p><p>Another special prosecutor, Brian Towne, was criminally charged after he joined the unit with misappropriating money confiscated by a rogue unit he created as LaSalle County state’s attorney to seize assets during traffic stops. The charges were dropped under speedy trial rules as Towne fought the case, which he claimed was retribution from a political rival.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Verónica Martinez/Injustice Watch</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Elward and Towne did not respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The Special Prosecution Unit is housed in an obscure, insular state agency, the Office of the Illinois State's Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor, or ILSAAP, which operates with little oversight.</p><p>ILSAAP has had just two directors over the past 35 years, including one whose two sons and grandson have held key positions in the office. The agency is exempt from the state Freedom of Information Act, not scrutinized by any inspector general and does not answer to the governor or the state attorney general.</p><p>Illinois is an outlier among states in having a unit of special prosecutors who try local government corruption cases without meaningful oversight from any elected official.</p><p>The board that governs the agency is made up of state’s attorneys from across Illinois — the very same officials who call on the special prosecutors to step in when they or their offices have a conflict of interest. But even they provide only superficial oversight, holding only brief periodic meetings.</p><p>And although ILSAAP was created to assist downstate prosecutors, its authority has expanded into Cook County criminal courts.</p><p>ILSAAP reviews every police-involved fatal shooting in Cook County when the state’s attorney declines charges, making an independent determination of whether charges against the officer are appropriate.</p><p>As of last year, ILSAAP had conducted 73 such reviews since 2016 and never overruled the Cook County state’s attorney’s decision not to charge, records show.</p><p>ILSAAP Director Patrick Delfino declined to comment. While the agency said it strives to be transparent, and Delfino provided basic data on cases the unit handled in 2024, he did not respond to detailed written questions.</p><p>Injustice Watch’s review found cases where special prosecutors obtained convictions and followed the law. Several attorneys in the unit have been praised for their work in underserved rural counties, including special prosecutors who have appeared in courts across the state to bring people charged with child sexual abuse to trial.</p><p>The unit as a whole handled a small fraction of the nearly 240,000 criminal cases filed statewide in 2024, and the wide range in the number and types of cases managed by Illinois’ more than 100 county prosecutors prevents any apples-to-apples comparison between the Special Prosecution Unit and local state’s attorney’s offices.</p><p>Yet unlike local prosecutors, Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit is not answerable to any one elected official, so there is little if any responsibility for patterns of civil rights violations and unjust outcomes.</p><p>"There's been a number of cases against innocent people brought by the special prosecutors,” says private investigator Bill Clutter, who helped clear four defendants wrongly accused of murder by the group.</p><p>“They’ve just been on the wrong side of justice,” he says.</p><p>To read the full Injustice Watch series, please go <a class="Link"
