entries.title: Funeral home shocker, pollution, mad bomber: Far South Side neighbors have been through a lot
entries.summary: <p>Jim Kinney has seen just about everything in his Far Southeast Side neighborhood: industrial waste that lit up the sky, the crime of the century, a mad bomber and a business that’s been allowed to fill the air with a stench that smells like rotting flesh.</p><p>Recently, just across the alley from his longtime home on 95th Street near Commercial Avenue, it was discovered that a funeral parlor neglected to care for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" >dozens of dead bodies</a> that were in various stages of decomposing.</p><p>“You can’t enjoy any outdoor things in the summer,” he says. “It smells like something died.”</p><p>Kinney is not describing South Chicago Chapel funeral home just behind his house, which was recently closed after the discovery of rotting bodies. He’s detailing a longtime nuisance that plagued the Far Southeast Side for decades: a feed-additive plant now operated by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" >Pullman Innovations</a>, which is being sued by residents and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/05/attorney-general-city-lawsuit-against-pullman-innovations-odors-kwame-raoul" >city and state authorities</a>.</p><p>This is the community of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/south-deering" >South Deering</a>, or as locals know it, Vet’s Park or Slag Valley — a nickname with roots in the steel-making heyday of Chicago. Decades ago, companies dumped molten metal left over from steelmaking into sites across the neighborhood. The waste product is known as slag, which is still prevalent throughout the area.</p><p>“We’d see the whole sky light up like a volcano,” Kinney says.</p><p>The 74-year-old Kinney, his dad and his grandfather all worked in the nearby mills, which mostly closed by the 1980s. There was Wisconsin Steel just to the south and U.S. Steel north of the home where he grew up along with 16 family members. You can’t talk about the Southeast Side without noting the legacy of the steel mills.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><div style="min-height:617px" id="datawrapper-vis-3kV22"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3kV22/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-3kV22"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3kV22/full.png" alt="Smells around South Deering (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Only about 20% of the larger South Deering neighborhood, which stretches from 95th Street on the north to 130th Street south, is residential. The remaining parts are industrial land, brownfields, wetlands or land reclaimed after the steel industry all but destroyed much of it decades ago.</p><p>The Slag Valley neighborhood and nearby Jeffrey Manor were also rocked by some of the most brutal crimes of the 20th century. Mass murderer Richard Speck killed eight student nurses in 1966 just a little more than a mile southwest of the funeral home.</p><p>In 1969, Frank Kulak, who lived across the back alley from Kinney’s family home, was arrested after a shootout with police that killed two officers. Kulak had planted homemade bombs across the Southeast Side, killing and injuring multiple people over a 20-month period.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> entries.title: Chicago Sinfonietta musicians have a new one-year deal, but performances are still paused
entries.summary: <p>Amid a trying moment for the local orchestra, the Chicago Sinfonietta and the players’ union, the Chicago Federation of Musicians, have agreed to a new, one-year contract.</p><p>But that contract, announced Thursday, arrives with only one performance on the horizon as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/07/chicago-sinfonietta-layoff-program-pause-finance-classical-music-2027https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/07/chicago-sinfonietta-layoff-program-pause-finance-classical-music-2027" target="_blank" ><u>the Sinfonietta has abruptly halted concerts and educational programming</u></a> and laid off administrative staff. The nearly 40-year-old group is known for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/08/chicago-sinfonietta-pause-financial-trouble-musicians-reaction-shock-diversity-classical" target="_blank" ><u>championing diverse musicians and composers</u></a>.</p><p>The players’ current three-year labor agreement was set to expire at the end of this month, and renewal was uncertain, given the Sinfonietta’s abrupt pause that started in the spring. Management calls it a “strategic renewal period” to focus on fundraising and sustainability planning.</p><p>“The agreement continues the long-standing collaborative labor relationship between the [Chicago Federation of Musicians] and the Chicago Sinfonietta, ensuring that a collective bargaining framework remains in place as the organization works to strengthen its financial foundation and chart its next chapter,” the union said in a statement.</p><p>BJ Levy, president of Chicago Federation of Musicians, Local 10-208 of the American Federation of Musicians, said Thursday that management bargained in good faith to reach the agreement, which includes a cost-of-living increase. “We’re pleased that we were able to get wage gains in this one-year period,” Levy said.</p><p>However, the 63 rostered musicians only get paid when they perform, which they haven’t done with the Sinfonietta since May.</p><p>The new agreement currently includes only one upcoming concert, to be held in January, in alignment with Martin Luther King Jr. Day and the group’s 40th anniversary. The Sinfonietta previously said it plans to present a fundraising event tied to MLK Day. However, the union noted Thursday that the concert has yet to be scheduled.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Additionally, the group received $245,000 in grants from the National Endowment for the Arts from 2019 to 2024 for new commissions, performances and educational activities.</p><p>In recent years, under the Trump administration, the NEA — the nation’s preeminent arts funder — has canceled grants to organizations, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/05/06/nea-grants-trump-chicago-cultural-event" target="_blank" ><u>including some in Chicago</u></a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/02/14/trump-nea-grants-national-endowment-arts-chicago-theater-dance" target="_blank" ><u>changed its grantmaking priorities</u></a>, with a prohibition on using federal monies for programs supporting “diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) that violate any applicable federal anti-discrimination laws.”</p><p>Levy said those changes at the federal level present a particular concern for Sinfonietta players and the future of the orchestra, founded by distinguished Black conductor Paul Freeman.</p><p>“It was quite unique in that Maestro Freeman founded the orchestra and was an African American conductor of great note, so that's what we're particularly concerned about,” Levy said. “In light of the federal government's outright attack on organizations that have a policy that is intended to promote underrepresented classes and include diversity, equity, inclusion in their mission statements.”</p><p>The union said it has received a commitment from the Sinfonietta to return to the table in March to negotiate for a new, three-year contract. The one-year deal is set to expire at the end of August 2027.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Earle Johnson, beer pioneer and welcoming owner of Quenchers tavern, dies at 83
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>As the owner of Quenchers, one of the city's first destination beer bars, Earle Johnson tapped into the power of nostalgia to draw customers.</p><p>Mr. Johnson stocked beer from nearly every country imaginable; when people returned from vacation — say in Argentina — and wanted to tap into the memory of drinking a beer on the beach, they could head to Quenchers in Logan Square and find that particular brew.</p><p>"I don't know how he did it. It was a lot of work carrying a beer that one person in 10,000 was interested in, but he was really good at creating his own niche market and a truly unique place, a place that people would go way out Western Ave., in 2003. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Brian Jackson/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mr. Johnson, who took ownership of the bar in 1981, was a beer pioneer decades before the microbrew craze swept the city and country.</p><p>"He was really, really ahead of the curve," Roeper said.</p><p>After putting 39 years of his life into Quenchers, at Fullerton and Western, the tavern closed in 2018. </p><p>Mr. Johnson, then 75, felt it was time, and sold the building. </p><p>A medical clinic is now where the bar used to be. </p><p>The space, prior to World War II, was an ice cream parlor. After the war it was turned into a bar and liquor store named Jug Full Liquors.</p><p>Mr. Johnson felt lucky to have sold two years before the pandemic hit the bar industry hard.</p><p>In retirement he read, traveled (including to Antarctica), spent time with his wife and two sons, and in recent months was putting the finishing touches on his dream home on the Northwest Side, but unfortunately never had the opportunity to move in.</p><p>Mr. Johnson died Aug. 4 following a heart attack. He was 83.</p><p>It's a wonder he ended up as a saloon keeper. His prior career trajectory was in Christian ministry.</p><p>Raised in Waukon, Iowa, a small town in the northeast corner of the state, Mr. Johnson attended Wheaton College, earned a master's degree from McCormick Theological Seminary and for several years worked in underserved Chicago communities as an outreach minister for Youth for Christ.</p><p>He shifted his focus to hospitality in his 30s after working at several restaurants, including The Berghoff in the Loop.</p><p>In 1979 he found himself bartending at Quenchers. Within months he became an investor and two years later owned the bar and building outright.</p><p>The bar was in a working class Polish and Hispanic area facing gentrification concerns, but Mr. Johnson made it clear that, in addition to welcoming traveling beer nerds, his place was a friendly neighborhood tavern.</p><p>It accrued regulars who had bar nicknames based on the simplest things about them, like "Old Man Bill." Another guy known as Whitey (the origin of the moniker is lost to time) folded the dollar bills he left on the bar as tips into origami animals.</p><p>"People felt at home there," said Cindy Weisbecker, a former patron and bartender who married another Quenchers bartender.</p><p>"I had a girl friend who'd stop there in the afternoon and balance her checkbook and just sit there have a coke because she knew it'd be a safe place where no would harass her, and that tone was set by Earle," she said.</p><p>"That's how I met Earle, he made me feel comfortable while I was at the bar waiting for my brother," said his wife, Nisa Johnson. "I brought up football, and no man could refuse to talk about football."</p><p>Scuffed wood, tin ceilings and old-fashioned glass-paneled cooler doors with latches that clicked shut provided ambiance. </p><p>"It was a place where a millionaire might be sitting next to some guy who just got out of jail, and the two could be talking and having a nice conversation," said David Weisbecker, who bartended there in the '80s.</p><p>In his younger days, if the mood struck, Mr. Johnson was known to perform somersaults down the length of the bar.</p><p>Though his work in Christian ministry never led him to head up a church, Mr. Johnson liked to say "This bar is my mission now, with a flock of a different kind."</p><p>He was a familiar and welcoming face to homeless people and others on the fringe of society who could depend on Mr. Johnson for a few bucks, a glass of orange juice, a working telephone and a safe place to sit for a while.</p><p>"He had a lot of empathy for people, especially people facing challenges, and he wanted to make people feel welcome and not out in the wilderness on their own," his wife said.</p><p>He was a longtime member of the Church of the Three Crosses in Old Town.</p><p>Quenchers was also known for its annual European Beer Tour, an event where Mr. Johnson issued "passports" complete with Polaroid photos that would be stamped at "Checkpoint Earle" after sampling beers from various countries.</p><p>There was also the Walk to Wrigley, in which dozens of people set off on foot from Quenchers on a pub crawl ending at the ballpark to take in a Cubs game.</p><p>An honorary street sign reading "Earle Johnson Way" was placed outside the bar before it closed.</p><p>In addition to his wife, Mr. Johnson is survived by his sons David Johnson and Dean Johnson.</p><p>A visitation will take place on Aug. 15 from 10 a.m. to noon at the Church of the Three Crosses, 333 W. Wisconsin St., in Old Town. It will be immediately followed by a funeral service from noon to 1:30 p.m.</p>

entries.title: 3 hurt in fiery Gold Coast wreck along North DuSable LSD
entries.summary: <p>Three people were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital after the car they were traveling in sideswiped another car, hit a median and burst into flames Thursday night in the Gold Coast neighborhood. </p><p>A blue car was going south in the 1000 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive around 9:05 p.m. when it sideswiped a black car going in the same direction, Chicago police said. </p><p>The blue car then slammed into a median and burst into flames, leaving three people in the blue car injured. </p><p>A 21-year-old woman and two men, 22 and 20, were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital for treatment, police said. Their conditions were not given by police. </p><p>The driver of the black sedan, a 45-year-old man, declined medical attention, officials said. </p><p>No further information was available. </p>
